title: Source Follower Frequency Response
intro: In a source follower $C_{GS}$ ties input to output, so the nodes interact and a one-pole-per-node picture fails. The useful results are the transfer function, the bootstrapped input capacitance, a negative input resistance with capacitive loads, and an output impedance that turns inductive.

blocks.text: Neglecting body effect and $r_o$, with $C_L$ the total output capacitance and $R_S$ the source resistance:

blocks.tex: \frac{V_{out}}{V_{in}} = \frac{g_m + C_{GS}s}{R_S(C_{GS}C_L + C_{GS}C_{GD} + C_{GD}C_L)s^2 + (g_m R_S C_{GD} + C_L + C_{GS})s + g_m}

blocks.text: The zero at $-g_m/C_{GS}$ is in the left half plane, near $\omega_T$: at high frequency $C_{GS}$ carries signal to the output with the same polarity as the transistor. If the poles are far apart the dominant one is

which reduces to $g_m/(C_L + C_{GS})$ for $R_S = 0$. With $C_L = 0$ the numerator cancels a factor and only the input pole $1/(R_S C_{GD})$ is left: with unity gate-to-source gain no current flows in $C_{GS}$, so it is bootstrapped away. A two-transistor variant (a follower whose bias device also amplifies) gives the same second-order form with extra terms.
Ignoring $C_{GD}$ (it simply shunts the input) and including body effect:

items: Low frequencies ($g_{mb} \gg |C_L s|$): $Z_{in} \approx 1/[C_{GS}s\,(1 + g_m/g_{mb})] + 1/g_{mb}$. The gate sees only $C_{GS}\,g_{mb}/(g_m + g_{mb})$ plus $C_{GD}$, a small fraction of $C_{GS}$. Miller's approximation with the gain $g_m/(g_m + g_{mb})$ gives the same.

High frequencies ($g_{mb} \ll |C_L s|$): $Z_{in} \approx \frac{1}{C_{GS}s} + \frac{1}{C_L s} + \frac{g_m}{C_{GS}C_L s^2}$. At $s = j\omega$ the last term is a negative resistance $-g_m/(C_{GS}C_L\omega^2)$ in series with $C_{GS}$ and $C_L$.

blocks.text: A follower driving a capacitive load presents a negative resistance at its input. With an inductive source (bond wire, package) this can oscillate; oscillators exploit exactly this effect.
Output impedance: the follower looks inductive
Neglecting $C_{GD}$ and body effect, a test source at the output gives

At DC $Z_{out} = 1/g_m$; at very high frequency $C_{GS}$ shorts gate to source and $Z_{out} \to R_S$. A buffer has $1/g_m < R_S$, so $|Z_{out}|$ rises with frequency: an inductive output. It is matched exactly by $R_2 = 1/g_m$ in series with $R_1 = R_S - 1/g_m$ in parallel with an inductor

blocks.alt: Left: a source follower M1 with its gate driven through RS, CGS between gate and source, and a current source IB as the load; the output impedance is measured at the source. Right: the equivalent network, R2 in series with the parallel combination of R1 and an inductor L.
blocks.caption: The follower's output impedance equals $R_2$ in series with $R_1 \parallel L$. $C_{GS}/g_m \approx 1/\omega_T$.

blocks.text: Consequences: a follower driving a large load capacitance can ring, since $L$ and $C_L$ form a lightly damped resonance. Used on purpose, a follower with a large gate resistor is an 'active inductor'; as the load of a CS stage it partly cancels $C_L$ and extends the bandwidth, at the cost of a $V_{GS}$ of headroom, and it is lossy (series $1/g_m$, parallel $R_S - 1/g_m$) and limited by the neglected $C_{GD}$.

blocks.title: Dominant pole of a follower
blocks.text: A follower has $g_m = 2\text{ mS}$, $R_S = 5\text{ k}\Omega$, $C_{GD} = 10\text{ fF}$, $C_{GS} = 80\text{ fF}$ and $C_L = 200\text{ fF}$. Estimate the dominant pole.
solution: $R_S C_{GD} = 50\text{ ps}$; $(C_L + C_{GS})/g_m = 280\text{ fF}/2\text{ mS} = 140\text{ ps}$.

blocks.title: Equivalent inductance
blocks.text: A follower with $g_m = 4\text{ mS}$ and $C_{GS} = 100\text{ fF}$ is driven from $R_S = 2\text{ k}\Omega$. Find $R_1$, $R_2$ and $L$ of the output network.

blocks.title: Bootstrapped input capacitance
blocks.text: A follower has $C_{GS} = 100\text{ fF}$, $g_m = 3\text{ mS}$, $g_{mb} = 0.6\text{ mS}$ and negligible load capacitance at low frequency. How much of $C_{GS}$ does the input see?

blocks.title: Negative input resistance
blocks.text: A follower with $g_m = 2\text{ mS}$, $C_{GS} = 50\text{ fF}$ drives $C_L = 200\text{ fF}$. Find the input resistance at 1 GHz (high-frequency limit).
blocks.answer: About $-5.1\text{ k}\Omega$ in series with $C_{GS}$ and $C_L$.
